opus-5.5.text:
I think reinforcement learning is, at its core, the most general formulation we have of learning from experience. When you train a model with pretraining, you're learning from data that someone else produced: the model observes the world through text, but it isn't acting in it. Reinforcement learning closes that loop. The model tries something, sees what happens, gets some signal about whether that was good or bad, and updates. That's much closer to how people actually get good at things. You don't learn to ride a bike or write a proof by reading about it. You learn by attempting it, failing, and adjusting.

What's been exciting over the last few years is that these two paradigms turned out to be complementary rather than competing. For a long time, RL on its own was incredibly sample-inefficient. You'd have agents playing Atari games for millions of frames to learn something a child picks up in minutes. The missing piece was prior knowledge. Pretraining gives you a model that already understands a lot about the world, so when you start doing RL on top of it, the exploration isn't random anymore. The model already has reasonable guesses, and RL sharpens those guesses into reliable skills. It teaches the model to reason for longer, to check its work, to backtrack when something isn't working.

The way I'd put it is that pretraining gives you knowledge, and reinforcement learning gives you competence. And the really open frontier now is making that experience loop richer: longer tasks, messier environments, feedback that isn't just a clean right-or-wrong answer. If we can get models learning effectively from the kind of ambiguous, extended experience that humans learn from, I think that's where a lot of the next big gains come from.

r001.rationale: It says learning to write a proof comes from attempting it, failing, and adjusting, and describes checking work and backtracking as skills RL teaches.

r002.rationale: It presents reinforcement learning as complementary to pretraining and predicts richer experience loops, but does not predict that researchers will develop approaches better than RL.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that reinforcement learning is just the most direct formalization we have of what learning from experience means. You act, something happens, and you update based on whether the outcome was good or bad. That's it. Everything else is machinery to make that loop actually work at scale.

What's interesting is how the field's relationship to that idea has changed. For a long time, RL was this somewhat niche thing. You'd train an agent in a simulator to play a game or control a robot arm, and the results were impressive but narrow. Then pretraining came along and the dominant mode became learning from a static corpus. You take all of human text, you predict the next token, and you get a model that knows an enormous amount but has never really done anything. It's learned from other people's experience, in a sense, but not its own.

And I think the thing we've collectively realized over the last couple of years is that those two are complementary rather than competing. Pretraining gives you a model with a huge amount of prior knowledge and a good sense of what's plausible. But there's a ceiling to what you can get from imitation alone. At some point the model has to try things, see what works, and get feedback that's grounded in reality rather than in what a human would have written. That's where RL comes back in, and it comes back in a much more powerful form because the starting point is so much better.

The reasoning models are the clearest example. You give the model a problem with a verifiable answer, you let it think for a while, and you reward it when it gets the answer right. Nobody wrote down the reasoning traces it ends up producing. It discovered them by trying, failing, and trying again. That's learning from experience in a very literal sense, and it produces capabilities that you just couldn't get by scaling up imitation.

So the way I'd frame it is that RL isn't a separate paradigm that sits next to learning from experience. It's the engine for it. The open question is how far you can push the kinds of experience the model gets. Math and code are easy because the feedback is clean. The harder and more interesting frontier is environments where the signal is noisier, longer-horizon, and closer to what people actually do in the world.

r001.rationale: The response presents reasoning on problems with verifiable answers, including math, as learning through trying, failing, and receiving feedback.

r002.rationale: It frames RL as the engine for learning from experience and discusses pushing it further; it does not predict that better approaches than RL will emerge.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning is one way of turning experience into learning. You try something, you observe the outcome, and you adjust what you do next. The important part is that you’re learning from the consequences of your own actions, rather than only from examples someone has already collected.

For a language model, that might mean attempting a problem, checking whether the solution works, and using that feedback to improve. If you’re writing code, for example, you can run it and see whether it passes the tests. That gives you a signal beyond whether the code looks plausible.

But learning from experience is broader than reinforcement learning. You also need to figure out what to explore and what feedback is meaningful. A failed attempt can be very informative, but only if the learning process can turn that failure into better behavior the next time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses trying actions and learning from their outcomes, but does not identify deep reflection on mathematical concepts as learning from experience.

r002.rationale: The response says learning from experience is broader than reinforcement learning, but does not predict that researchers will develop better approaches than reinforcement learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning is a way of turning experience into learning. You try something, you see what happens, and you use that feedback to change what you do next. The important part is that you’re not being told the right action at every step. You may only find out much later whether your approach worked.

For a language model, that means going beyond learning from examples of what people have written. The model can attempt a problem, get feedback on the result, and gradually learn which approaches are useful. If it writes code, for example, it can run that code and see whether the tests pass.

But experience alone isn’t enough. You need an environment that gives you meaningful feedback, and you need a way to learn from it. So I see reinforcement learning as one important piece of learning from experience—the mechanism that lets the consequences of your actions improve your future behavior.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning through actions, feedback, and consequences, but does not identify deep reflection on mathematical concepts as learning from experience.

r002.rationale: The response calls reinforcement learning one important piece of learning from experience, but does not predict researchers will develop better approaches than it.
